content: Borage, scientifically known as Borago officinalis L., is an annual herb that is also referred to as starflower. It originates from Syria but has become naturalized across the Mediterranean region, much of Europe, North Africa, and Iran. The plant typically grows to a height of 60–100 cm (2–3 feet) and is covered in bristly hairs on its stems and leaves. Its leaves are alternate, simple, and measure 5–15 cm (2–6 inches) in length. The flowers are small, blue or pink, and feature five narrow, triangular-pointed petals. Borage exhibits an indeterminate growth habit, which allows it to produce numerous seeds, often leading to its prolific spread beyond the area where it was initially planted. In regions with milder climates, borage can bloom continuously for most of the year. However, its leaves contain small amounts of liver-toxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids, including intermedine, lycopsamine, amabiline, and supinine, at a concentration of approximately 10 ppm in the dried herb. The leaves of borage have a flavor reminiscent of fresh cucumber and are commonly used in salads and soups, particularly in Germany. One well-known recipe featuring borage is Frankfurt Green Sauce (Frankfurter Grüne Soße), which is made from seven herbs: parsley, chervil, chives, cress, sorrel, burnet, and borage. Additionally, borage is a traditional ingredient in the recipe for a Pimm's Cup. In the Spanish regions of Aragón and Navarra, borage is also a popular culinary ingredient. A simple preparation involves cooking winter-grown borage (which has a better flavor due to slower growth) with potatoes in boiling water before seasoning the dish with olive oil and salt. The flowers of borage, which contain the non-toxic pyrrolizidine alkaloid thesinine, have a sweet, honey-like taste and are often used to decorate desserts and dishes. Dried borage flowers are also used to make tea, a traditional calming beverage in Iran. This tea has a rich purple color that turns bright pink when a few drops of lemon juice are added. Borage is notable for being the highest known plant-based source of gamma-linolenic acid (GLA), a polyunsaturated fatty acid (18:3, cis-6,9,12-octadecatrienoic acid). The oil extracted from its seeds is marketed as starflower oil or borage oil. This oil is also rich in oleic and palmitic acids, which contribute to its hypocholesterolemic (cholesterol-lowering) effects. Recently commercialized, borage oil is believed to regulate metabolism and the hormonal system. Many naturopathic practitioners recommend it as a remedy for premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and menopause symptoms, such as hot flashes. Additionally, borage is sometimes used to alleviate and support recovery from colds, bronchitis, and respiratory infections due to its anti-inflammatory and balsamic properties. The flowers can be prepared as an infusion to harness their medicinal benefits. As a companion plant, borage is not only an attractive, flowering, and edible herb but also enhances the flavor of nearby tomato vines when grown within a few feet of them.
